output:
*Interview with Dr Casimir Vauthier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Thank you for staying up, Doctor. First, how long have you been at the Monniers' house?

DR VAUTHIER: Thirty years, Inspector, as the family's physician and their friend. I am there whenever I am asked, and tonight I was asked to dine. Aurèle liked his friends about him at the turn of the year, and he made no exception for his old doctor.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the dinner.

DR VAUTHIER: You will have heard how it was done, so I shall be brief. When the temple struck nine, Aurèle made each of us show him our watches, as he does every year, and he told each of us what was wrong with ours. Mine, he said, was two minutes ahead of the bell. He was very pleased to tell me so. Aurèle has always enjoyed being right about other people's watches.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

DR VAUTHIER: Madame and I played piquet in the salon. Odile plays the game with a severity I admire and do not always survive. We played until a quarter to eleven by my watch, when I went out to the hall to fetch my cigar case from my coat. I was not going to smoke in Madame's salon without her leave.

MATTHEY: What happened while you were in the hall?

DR VAUTHIER: Madame began to play the piano as I went out. It was Chopin, as it generally is with her. She stopped when I came back.

MATTHEY: And after that?

DR VAUTHIER: We went on with the cards. The temple struck ten while we were still at them. I looked at the salon clock, and it showed five minutes to ten. I remarked on it to Madame, and we played on.

MATTHEY: Tell me about Monsieur Monnier's work.

DR VAUTHIER: He would talk of nothing but that repeater. He meant it to strike the first minute of the new century, and he told anyone who would listen. I used to tease him that a watch should be allowed to keep its own counsel. He never saw the joke.

MATTHEY: You have seen his body?

DR VAUTHIER: I have. There is a blow to the back of the head, Inspector, struck from behind, and it was heavy. I would say he knew very little of it. Death would have been very quick.

MATTHEY: And the regulator in the atelier?

DR VAUTHIER: It stopped with its master. I find I cannot say it any other way, and I am too old to try.

MATTHEY: You attended Monsieur Jules Monnier as well.

DR VAUTHIER: In 1889, in his last illness. It was a hard death, and the family has never spoken of it much. Félix was a boy then, and Aurèle carried the grief quietly, the way he carried everything.

MATTHEY: Is there anything about tonight you think I should know?

DR VAUTHIER: Only what I have told you. I have no opinions about the watches, and I have no wish to guess at what I did not see. *Tempus edax rerum*, Inspector. I have always thought it a poor epitaph for a watchmaker.

MATTHEY: Is there anything else you wish to add?

DR VAUTHIER: Only that Madame has had a great deal to bear tonight, and I hope you will be gentle with her.
